content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.persian-persian-literature-volume-1-gutenberg-l8269-l8388","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/persian/project-gutenberg/persian-literature-volume-1.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INVASION OF IRN BY AFRSIYB / THE RETURN OF KAI-KS / STORY OF SOHRB / THE STORY OF SAIWUSH; lines 8269-8388","start":"8269","end":"8388","translation":"Persian Literature, Volume 1","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"At King Ks's court, Ts argues that Frburz, identified as the heir, should succeed if Ks leaves the throne, while Gdarz argues that Kai-khosru should replace the murdered eldest son Saiwush. Ks tests Frburz and Khosru by ordering each to conquer the fire-emitting demon-fortress Bahmen. Frburz and Ts fail after their forces are burned and cannot enter the airborne fortress. Khosru, guided by knowledge received in a heavenly dream, writes God's name on his javelin, displays it with Gw, prays, breaks the fortress's sorcery, defeats demons, enters the fortress, and builds a temple after victory.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ts declares allegiance to Ks and says that, if Ks lays aside the throne and diadem, his loyalty will be owed to Frburz as heir rather than to a stranger.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gdarz says that Saiwush, the king's eldest son, was unjustly murdered and argues that Kai-khosru should be put in his place.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ks says that he loves his children alike and seeks to prevent disunion and preserve brotherly kindness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ks orders Frburz and Khosru to attack Bahmen, a demon-fortress continually issuing fire, and makes the conqueror sovereign of Persia.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Frburz and Ts reach a fortress surrounded by fire and hot wind; they see it in mid-air with no visible gate or door, lose many warriors, and return unsuccessful after a week.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Khosru recognizes the blazing fortress as sorcery and has previously learned in a heavenly dream how to destroy magical charms.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Khosru writes God's war.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Lohursp relinquishes authority, adopts a recluse's coarse clothing, retires to a pilgrimage place near Balkh, and spends the rest of his life in prayer and worship.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage says earlier sovereigns worshipped God and portrays the ill Lohursp to health; Gushtsp subsequently becomes Zerdusht's disciple.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Zerdusht represents that he has visited heaven and hell, knows the seven celestial mansions through an attendant angel, and has received the Zendavesta from above.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Zerdusht further Zarr is killed by the demon Bai-derafsh; Gushtsp promises Isfendiyr the crown if he defeats the demon and enemy. Isfendiyr kills Bai-derafsh and helps rout Arjsp's forces. Gushtsp commemorates Zarr with a monument and perpetual lights, promotes fire worship and Zerdusht's religion, and later crowns Isfendiyr.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The invading force plunders settlements, burns villages and buildings, uproots trees, and advances under a darkness that conceals its movement.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"At Zerdusht's direction, Gushtsp asks his vizier Jamsp about the horoscope; Jamsp predicts that many of the king's relatives and warriors will die, but that Gushtsp will ultimately win.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The opposing forces pray before battle; arrows darken the sky, and the battle is described with dark clouds above and blood-red ground below.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ardshr and his brother Shydasp are killed in the fighting. Zarr kills many opponents but is killed by the demon Bai-derafsh.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Gushtsp promises Isfendiyr his crown and throne if Isfendiyr kills Bai-derafsh and defeats the enemy, and gives him the black horse Behzd.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Isfendiyr kills Bai-derafsh with a spear, cuts off the demon's head, and gives the head and Zarr's armor to Bish. The first identifies the beloved as the sole presence in the speaker's shrine of affection and equates divine presence across the Ka'bah and wine-house. The second praises Farrukh's appearance. The third describes the rose's spring emergence and short bloom, calls for wine, music, and companionship, and invokes Zoroaster, Nimrod, Christ, Solomon, David, and Mahmud.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker says that the world has grown wearying and that the shrine of affection contains no Being but the speaker's friend.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker says that an exhalation from the beloved's garden would make the heart burst its bud-like veil in joy.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker tells a secluded zealot not to blame and says that the arch of the Mihrb is found in an eyebrow's bow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker states that no difference is seen between the Ka'bah and the wine-house because He is equally present wherever the speaker looks.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The poem describes a Kalandar's manner of computing the Path and contrasts one who gives only a hair's head with a genuine Kalandar who gives his head.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The speaker repeatedly expresses desire and yearning for Farrukh and describes Farrukh through hair, cheek, knee, mien, brow, curl, and grace.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The third poem says that the rose springs from Nothing into Being, while the violet bends low at the rose's feet.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The third poem calls for refreshment from a cup, wine, music, kissing Sk, and remaining with wine, harp, and charmer until the rose's bloom has passed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The third poem compares the rose's brief bloom to the passing days of life and says that earth rivals the Immortal Garden during the rose and lily's reign, though the immortal is sought on earth in vain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The third poem calls for Zoroaster's worship to revive in gardens and says that the fires of Nimrod are alive within tulip blossoms.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The third poem associates the rose with Solomon riding a windy courser and the Bird with David's melodies at morning.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The speaker requests a replenished goblet in Solomon's dominion and pledges Mahmud, described as Vizir, the cycle's saf, and the column of the Faith.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Hfiz / first-person poetic speaker","description":"A first-person speaker appears
